Infidel
ĭn'fĭ-dəl
n. (an unbeliever; one who has no part with him that believeth)
Latin infidelis, unfaithful, from in-, not, and fidelis, faithful. The Greek apistos is the plain negative of pistos, believing — the man without faith.

Biblical Definition

The word occurs twice in the Authorized Version, and both places are startling. Paul asks the Corinthians a chain of questions with only one answer: “And what concord hath Christ with Belial? or what part hath he that believeth with an infidel?” (2Co 6:15). The infidel there is not a man of another religion in the modern sense but simply the unbeliever, and the apostle's point is that the believer and the unbeliever have no shared foundation on which to be unequally yoked. The second use is the one that stops a professing man in his tracks: “But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel” (1Ti 5:8). Paul does not say such a man is like an infidel; he says he is worse, because the unbeliever who feeds his family at least keeps the natural duty that even a fallen conscience acknowledges, while the professor who neglects his has denied by his hands what he confesses with his mouth. Titus states the principle flatly: “They profess that they know God; but in works they deny him” (Tit 1:16). Faith that provides nothing has confessed nothing.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines an infidel as one who disbelieves the inspiration of the Scriptures and the divine origin of Christianity; a disbeliever, distinguished from the heathen who has never had the gospel.

expand to see more

INFIDEL, a. [L. infidelis; in and fidelis, faithful.] Unbelieving; disbelieving the inspiration of the Scriptures, or the divine institution of Christianity.

INFIDEL, n. One who disbelieves the inspiration of the Scriptures, and the divine origin of Christianity.

The word is not applied to the heathen who have never heard the gospel, but to those who reject it.

He hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel. 1 Tim. v.

Key Scripture

2Co 6:15 — "And what concord hath Christ with Belial? or what part hath he that believeth with an infidel?"

1Ti 5:8 — "But if any provide not for his own, and specially for those of his own house, he hath denied the faith, and is worse than an infidel."

Tit 1:16 — "They profess that they know God; but in works they deny him, being abominable, and disobedient, and unto every good work reprobate."

Rom 1:28 — "And even as they did not like to retain God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do those things which are not convenient;"

Modern Corruption

1 Timothy 5:8 measures a man's creed by his provision for his own house, and that measurement is quietly dropped wherever unbelief is treated as a merely intellectual position.

expand to see more

Unbelief is habitually presented as a conclusion honestly reached — a man weighed the evidence and was not persuaded — and on that account as morally neutral. Romans 1 refuses the account. Men did not like to retain God in their knowledge; the mind was given over because the will had already turned. Unbelief is therefore not the absence of a proof but the suppression of one, and Scripture treats it as culpable throughout. This matters pastorally because the neutral account produces a limp evangelism that argues a man into assent and never calls him to repent, when the New Testament everywhere commands both together: repent, and believe the gospel. The apostle's question in 2 Corinthians is likewise not a counsel about compatibility but a statement about foundations. Christ and Belial have no concord, and where there is no concord there can be no yoke.

The sharper corruption is the one 1 Timothy 5:8 was written against, and it runs in the professing church rather than outside it. A man may hold every article of the confession, attend faithfully, speak well of the doctrines of grace, and leave his own household unprovided for — and Paul's verdict is that he has denied the faith and stands worse than an unbeliever. The verse cuts two ways in our own moment. It rebukes the man who spends himself on ministry or on reputation while his wife and children go without his labour, and it rebukes the notion that a family's support is a matter of preference or of arrangement rather than a duty laid on the head of the house. The word provide is wide: bread, protection, instruction, and the ordering of a household under God. Where the doctrine is confessed and the door of one's own house is neglected, the doctrine has been denied in the only language the neighbours can read.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek apistos (G571), unbelieving, faithless, rendered infidel in both Authorized Version occurrences; from a-, not, and pistis (G4102), faith.

expand to see more

Greek apistos (G571) — without faith, unbelieving; rendered infidel at 2 Corinthians 6:15 and 1 Timothy 5:8, and unbeliever elsewhere.

Greek pistis (G4102) — faith, the thing the infidel lacks and the professor of 1 Timothy 5:8 is said to have denied.

Greek arneomai (G720) — to deny, to disown; used of the man who does not provide for his own; 1 Timothy 5:8, 2 Timothy 2:12.

Greek heterozugeo (G2086) — to be unequally yoked, the figure of two beasts of different kinds under one bar; 2 Corinthians 6:14.

Greek Belial (G955) — worthlessness, a name for the evil one set opposite Christ in the same verse; 2 Corinthians 6:15.

Usage

"“What part hath he that believeth with an infidel?” — no shared foundation, therefore no yoke."

"“Worse than an infidel” — the professor who leaves his own house unprovided."

"“In works they deny him” — the confession the neighbours can actually read."
